extracted.intended_audience: empirical IP scholars, patent litigators, law professors, and policy analysts studying patent litigation outcomes
extracted.subtask_description: Hand-coding and empirical analysis of federal district-court patent lawsuits (filed 2008–2009) at the patent–case level, classifying merits rulings, trial outcomes, and patent/industry/technology characteristics for regression analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case inclusion window
rubrics_metrics.description: Include all patent lawsuits filed in a federal district court between January 1, 2008 and December 31, 2009.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selected because those years provide a snapshot of current litigation while leaving sufficient time for cases to be finally resolved; coding performed in late summer/fall 2013 when only ~2%–3% of cases remained open.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case inclusion criteria (subject-matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include only lawsuits that include a complaint for infringement of a utility patent, or declaratory relief of noninfringement or invalidity of a utility patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude inventorship and licensing disputes, malpractice actions, allegations of design or plant patent infringement, and other non-utility-patent matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum-case-event inclusion (decision/appeal)
rubrics_metrics.description: From Lex Machina lists, include lawsuits that contained at least one ruling on summary judgment or trial; also include cases with an appeal but without a summary judgment ruling or trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The second list (appeals without SJ/trial) captures cases resolved by stipulation based on claim construction to preserve an appeal route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of analysis: patent–case combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a patent–case combination as the unit of analysis and code the outcome separately for each asserted patent in a lawsuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a jury returned a verdict on two patents, record separately for each patent; when different claims of a single patent have different substantive outcomes, create new records for each group of claims with differing outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary data source selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Lex Machina as the primary data source because it provides cleaned, indexed access to PACER litigation documents and identifies summary judgment rulings, trial events, and appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on raw Administrative Office PACER data due to classification errors; Lex Machina includes lawsuits even without decisions on Westlaw/Lexis and reduces raw-data errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document review and manual coding standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Read all relevant orders, opinions, motions, verdicts, appellate rulings, and other necessary court documents on a docket to code litigation outcomes accurately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manual review is necessary because many dockets are extremely complicated (often >500 entries); coders must resolve ambiguous or terse opinions by reading underlying party briefing where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coder qualifications and procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use experienced patent litigators (not student coders) to hand-code outcomes because coding patent-case outcomes requires deep knowledge of patent law and litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemley and Schwartz personally coded approximately half the lawsuits each; they overlapped coding on roughly 10% (and additional random overlap) to permit inter-coder reliability assessment and to fine-tune the codebook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-coder reliability measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess coding reliability using an agreement coefficient (Cohen’s Kappa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report kappa for key variables (e.g., definitive/interim winners kappa = 0.9534; SJ invalidity/non-infringement kappa ≈ 0.9793); revisit overlapping dockets to correct disagreements and document corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding of summary judgment rulings (inclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capture all rulings on summary judgment relating to patent-law issues, including motions of summary judgment of noninfringement, infringement, validity/invalidity, inequitable conduct, and no inequitable conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude rulings on issues that are not patent-specific (e.g., laches) and exclude SJ rulings if the court did not reach the merits (e.g., denied as premature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Final-resolution coding rules
rubrics_metrics.description: If a summary-judgment ruling is granted on an issue, code that SJ as the final resolution for that issue; denials of SJ are not final resolutions (they indicate disputed issues of material fact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an issue is later resolved at trial, the trial resolution becomes the final coding; if the Federal Circuit reverses on appeal, update the final-resolution coding to reflect the appellate decision. Retain original SJ coding in the SJ dataset even if later reversed so as to capture trial-court SJ win rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim vs definitive wins
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify decisions that finally rule for a party on an issue as 'definitive wins' and rulings that rule for a party but keep the issue alive (e.g., denial of SJ, remand) as 'interim wins'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction helps separate final outcomes from procedural or partial victories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Granular invalidity-ground coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Code invalidity rulings by specific legal ground: utility, patentable subject matter (section 101), section 102 (prior art/anticipation), obviousness (section 103), indefiniteness (section 112 ¶2), written description, enablement, and best mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also code various bases for section 102 invalidity separately where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Granular infringement-type coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Capture infringement determinations by type: literal infringement, doctrine of equivalents (DOE), and various forms of indirect infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record separate entries for each basis on which the court ruled so that multiple grounds in a single lawsuit appear independently in the dataset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unenforceability and inequitable-conduct coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Code findings of unenforceability and the particular basis for unenforceability (e.g., inequitable conduct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include both grants and denials related to unenforceability arguments and their underlying factual/legal bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of moot summary-judgment issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not include summary-judgment rulings that the court denied as moot in the merits coding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if the court grants anticipation on the merits and denies obviousness as moot, include anticipation but not obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology-area classification procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign each patent a single primary technology area (mechanical, electronics, chemistry, biotechnology, software, optics) focusing primarily on claim language, aided by written description and drawings; identify secondary technology areas when another technology forms an additional integral part of the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roughly one-third of patents had a secondary technology; primary areas are mutually exclusive; when necessary consult technical dictionaries/encyclopedias/Internet but only rarely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of primary technology areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Define technology categories by the nature of the claimed invention: (1) Mechanical — claims cover mechanical parts/power-transfer techniques; (2) Electronics — claims cover traditional electronic circuitry or storage/transmission of electric energy; (3) Chemistry — claims cover chemical reactions, compounds, proportions, metal alloys/nonmetallic composites (small-molecule chemistry; exclude large molecules placed in biotech); (4) Biotechnology — claims cover processes involving advanced genetic techniques, products created by them, or their use in biotech research; (5) Software — claims cover data processing (manipulation of data); (6) Optics — claims cover use of light waves or light energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For biotechnology, do not disaggregate genetic-engineering techniques into separate tech areas for this study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software business-method subset definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Define 'software business methods' as a narrow subset of software patents whose claims obviously cover automated generation of customer proposals, advertising, financial techniques, use of online catalogs, and similar business-transaction techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include computer-controlled manufacturing methods in the business-method category; because business-method is a subset of software, treat it appropriately in regressions (cannot co-include with broader software unless substituting categories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry classification procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign patents to industry categories that focus on the business use of the patent and the industry of the patent owner; use claim language, written description, and extrinsic evidence (especially the Internet) to determine the industry category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technology and industry classifications differ: technology refers to nature of invention while industry refers to owner/use; in some cases (e.g., biotechnology) the same term may be used for both, but they are not identical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling multiple issues per patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Include merits rulings on every distinct issue litigated to decision for each patent, whether or not the ruling resulted in a trial outcome or a grant of summary judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an accused infringer argued multiple invalidity grounds and the court denied some but granted others, record each ruling (except moot denials) so the dataset reflects all merits rulings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for non-independence in regression
rubrics_metrics.description: When running regressions, account for lack of independence among observations (multiple patents per case, same patent litigated multiple times, consolidated cases) by clustering standard errors on the unique patent numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clustering adjusts inference for correlated observations arising from litigation structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording trial specifics and appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Record whether there was a jury or bench trial, decisions on post-verdict JMOL motions, whether an appeal was lodged, and how the appeal was resolved (affirmed, reversed, pending, dismissed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When trial or appellate opinions lack sufficient detail to ascertain the basis for a ruling, read the underlying briefing by the parties to capture basis accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale for year selection and case completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Select filing years such that most cases will have reached final resolution by the time of coding to minimize right-censoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors chose 2008–2009 because by coding in 2013 only a small percentage of cases remained open, enabling comprehensive outcome measurement.
